nameStory: The bobcat gets its name from its most distinctive feature - that short, stubby tail that looks like it's been "bobbed" or cut off. This abbreviated tail, typically only 4-7 inches long, ends with a black tip and gives this wild cat its memorable common name.
description: The bobcat is New England's only native wild cat, roughly twice the size of a house cat with a muscular, compact build. Adults can reach up to 4 feet in total length and weigh 15-35 pounds, with males being larger than females. Their tawny brown to gray fur is spotted with darker markings, and they have distinctive tufted ears, facial ruffs, and that signature short, black-tipped tail that sets them apart from any domestic cat.

idTips.label: Tail
idTips.description: Short, stubby tail only 4-7 inches long with distinct black tip on top and white underneath - looks chopped off compared to a house cat's long tail

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Stocky, muscular build about twice the size of a house cat with long legs that give it a high-shouldered appearance when walking

idTips.label: Fur
idTips.description: Tawny brown to gray coat with dark spots or bars, distinctive black bars on the forelegs, and a white belly with black spots

idTips.label: Tracks
idTips.description: Round paw prints about 2 inches wide with four toes and retractable claws that rarely show; walking pattern shows hind feet stepping in front foot prints

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves with fluid, silent grace through thick cover; often sits motionless for long periods when hunting, then pounces with explosive speed

idTips.label: Sign
idTips.description: Scat is segmented and rope-like, often containing fur and bones; claw marks on trees about 3-4 feet high where they stretch and mark territory

habitat: Bobcats thrive in mixed forests with dense understory, rocky outcrops, and brushy areas that provide cover for hunting. They prefer edge habitats where forests meet fields or wetlands, and are increasingly found in suburban areas with sufficient wooded corridors. Look for them in areas with abundant rabbit and rodent populations, particularly around stone walls, fallen logs, and thick bramble patches.

seasonality.spring: Peak breeding season when you might hear their loud yowling calls at night; kittens are born in dens under rock ledges or in hollow logs.
seasonality.summer: Most active at dawn and dusk, hunting in open areas; their spotted coat is shorter and more visible during this season.
seasonality.fall: Increasing activity as they hunt to build fat reserves; young bobcats disperse from their mother's territory, making sightings more likely.
seasonality.winter: Develop thick, grayish winter coat; tracks in snow are the most common sign, following deer trails and rabbit runs through the woods.

funFact: A bobcat can leap up to 12 feet horizontally to catch prey and can run up to 30 mph in short bursts - they're such powerful jumpers they can take down deer several times their own weight by leaping onto their backs!
confusionNotes: Most often confused with large house cats, but remember the "stubby tail test" - if the tail is longer than 7 inches, it's not a bobcat. Canada lynx have much larger, heavily furred snowshoe-like paws and longer ear tufts, but are extremely rare in New England.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "wildcat" in some regions, bobcats are actually lynx species, not true wildcats. Many reported "mountain lion" sightings in New England are actually bobcats, which can appear much larger when seen briefly in poor lighting conditions.
compareHints: Bobcats differ from their close relative the Canada lynx by having smaller paws, shorter ear tufts, and a more brownish (rather than grayish) coat. Unlike Canada lynx which specialize in hunting snowshoe hares, bobcats are generalist predators. Bobcats' hind legs are also proportionally shorter, giving them a less lanky appearance than the long-legged lynx.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to their close relative the bobcat, Canada lynx are generally larger with much more prominent features—bigger paws, longer ear tufts, and longer legs.
